question_en:
A company reports under US GAAP and provides the following information on its equipment:

| Metric | $ |
|---|---|
| Carrying amount | 31,000 |
| Expected future cash flows: Undiscounted | 28,000 |
| Expected future cash flows: Present value | 26,500 |
| Fair value if sold | 22,000 |
| Cost to sell | 2,500 |

Due to an impairment charge, the carrying value of the machine is closest to:
explanation_en:
Impairment charges are recognized when an asset's carrying amount, measured as historical cost minus accumulated depreciation, is greater
than its recoverable value. US GAAP defines the recoverable amount as simply the undiscounted expected future cash flows. In this case,
the carrying amount ($31,000) exceeds the recoverable amount ($28,000).
The impaired asset is written down to a new carrying value with a new depreciation schedule. Under US GAAP, the asset would be written down
to fair value (ie, value if sold [$22,000]). This fair value estimate becomes the new carrying amount.
In contrast, IFRS defines the recoverable amount and the new carrying value as the greater of the asset's fair value less costs to sell the asset
($22,000 − $2,500) or the discounted future cash flows ($26,500) that the asset is expected to generate (Choices A and C).

question_en: The following applies to a one-year forward contract: If the present value of the costs of holding the underlying asset for 1 year is ¥1.62, then the present value of the benefits of holding the asset (in ¥) is closest to:
explanation_en: An owner of an asset is exposed to the risk that the commodity price will fall between now and when it is sold. Selling an asset forward means that the seller commits to deliver that asset at a future date for a guaranteed price. Selling forward eliminates the seller's price risk, but it also means that the seller does not benefit if the asset's spot price is higher than the contracted price when the contract expires. Although the price the farmer receives at expiration is guaranteed, the relative value of the contract varies prior to expiration depending on how spot prices of the underlying asset change. At expiration, the value of the contract is the difference between the spot price and the forward price. Prior to that time, the contract's value is the difference between the asset's current spot price and the present value of the forward price. Any gain to one party from a change in the forward contract's value is exactly offset by the other party's loss. In this example, any increase in spot wheat prices prior to expiration causes the contract's value to increase to the long party. As the farmer is short, an increase in the contract's value represents a loss. (Choice B) The price that the farmer receives at the contract's expiration does not change, but the value of the contract changes as the underlying asset's price changes. (Choice C) The value of any contract to the short party increases only if the price of the underlying asset decreases.

subtopic: 8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives
question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two 18-month forward contracts, each for a different underlying asset: If the risk-free rate is 2.8%, the forward price of Asset Y is most likely:
option_a: less than the forward price of Asset X.
option_b: equal to the forward price of Asset X.
option_c: greater than the forward price of Asset X.
explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in Arbitrage-free derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and Replication risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives Risk-neutral and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Derivative pricing is based on three key concepts: Arbitrage-free pricing assumes market prices are free of arbitrage opportunities. Derivative pricing is risk-neutral since arbitrage-free markets guarantee risk-free positions that earn the risk-free rate. Equivalent positions can be created through replication using combinations of the underlying asset, a risk-free asset, and a derivative. Derivative prices must reflect the risk-free rate since riskless positions can be created by combining an underlying asset (eg, long a bond) with related derivatives (eg, short bond futures). Similarly, derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying asset with the risk-free asset. Replicated positions that are economically equivalent should trade at economically equivalent prices. Thus, the price of a derivative reflects the value of a replication strategy. If an economically equivalent condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that riskless profits can no longer be earned and arbitrage-free pricing is achieved. This arbitrage-free pricing renders investors risk-neutral, meaning that the risk premiums required by investors to hold the underlying asset have no effect on derivative pricing (Choice B). (Choice C) The price of a derivative contract is dependent on the price of the underlying asset and the terms of the contract, such as the strike price and exercise date. This does not imply that the underlying asset's expected rate of return will be the same as the derivative's expected rate of return.

option_b: the risk-free rate since riskless positions should earn a risk-free rate of return.
option_c: the underlying's required rate of return since the derivative's expected returns must be the
explanation_en:
Derivative pricing concepts
Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives
Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in
Arbitrage-free derivatives and underlying assets
Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated
(ie, no-arbitrage pricing)
Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and
Replication risk-free assets
Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns

Derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying with the risk-free asset. Economically equivalent positions should
trade at prices that result in equal returns. If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer
be earned. Arbitrage-free pricing means that investor risk aversion has no impact on derivative pricing. Therefore, derivative pricing is described
as risk-neutral pricing.
By combining positions in the underlying asset (eg, long bond) and the derivative (eg, short bond futures), investors can create riskless
positions. Since riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return, the expected payoffs are discounted at the risk-free rate when pricing
derivatives.
(Choice A) An absence of arbitrage profits means derivatives are fairly priced relative to the underlying asset. In that case, taking offsetting
positions in the derivative and an appropriate replication strategy earns the risk-free rate of return, resulting in the risk-free rate (not zero) being
the appropriate discount rate.
(Choice C) An asset's required rate of return is appropriate for valuing assets but not for pricing derivatives. Derivative prices are derived from
their underlying asset's price, based on arbitrage and risk-neutral pricing; therefore, the asset's required rate of return is not the appropriate
discount rate.

question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two competitors, concerning their differences in accounting methods. To facilitate proper financial comparison, the analyst should most appropriately:
option_a: adjust Company 2's gross book value of fixed assets.
option_b: reduce Company 1's net income for fair value investment gains.
option_c: reduce Company 1's amount of intangible assets by its goodwill balance.
explanation_en: High-quality financial earnings are characterized by sustainability over future periods. The quality of reported earnings tends to be positively correlated to the quality of the financial statements that chronicle those earnings. Companies with conservative accounting policies tend to generate high-quality earnings more often than companies with more aggressive reporting methods. The same applies for companies that make unbiased accounting choices. Pro forma statements are one characteristic of aggressive reporting. They selectively present limited information that makes current earnings appear stronger than might otherwise be justified. The selective nature of the information calls into question whether the earnings are sustainable. Pro forma presentations do not comply with either US GAAP or IFRS. Choosing shorter useful lives for noncurrent assets represents a conservative accounting choice (Choice C). The shorter lives result in higher depreciation expense each year. The increased expense means lower earnings. Also, shorter useful lives implicitly signal the company's intent to invest in its infrastructure to foster future earnings growth. (Choice B) Revenue is the primary driver of earnings. Robust and sustainable revenues tend to result in consistent, high-quality earnings.

question_en: Which of the following reporting practices is most likely considered aggressive accounting?
option_a: Presenting pro forma earnings per share (EPS) that are lower than reported EPS.
option_b: Capitalizing, instead of expensing, in-process research and development (R&D) costs.
option_c: Using the criteria of available-for-sale securities, rather than trading securities, to treat bond
explanation_en: Under both IFRS and US GAAP, revenue can be recognized when the risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer. When goods are in transit: under Free on Board (FOB) destination, ownership transfers to the buyer when the shipped goods are received. Therefore, the seller can recognize revenue only when the goods arrive at the customer's destination. under FOB shipping point, ownership transfers to the buyer upon shipment. Therefore, the seller can recognize revenue when the goods are shipped. For a seller, switching shipping terms from FOB destination to FOB shipping will change the timing of when the goods' ownership is transferred, thus changing when revenue can be recognized. It effectively allows a seller to recognize revenue earlier, which results in more reported revenue for the current period. Therefore, management sometimes uses this tactic to enhance reported revenue for a period. (Choice A) Expensing, rather than capitalizing, an asset purchase will increase operating expenses for the current period, thus lowering profits. Expensing an asset purchase is a conservative choice. (Choice B) Decreasing future cash benefit projections in a goodwill impairment test will more likely lead to a write-down; therefore, it is a conservative choice.

explanation_en: Common warning signs of accounting manipulation Frequent reporting "surprises" "Nonrecurring" items that consistently appear in multiple periods Unusual levels of receivables, payables, inventory turnover, operating cash flow, net income, profit margins Underestimating warranty expenses that are "restated" in subsequent periods Useful lives for long-term assets that are different than industry average Related-party transactions Heavy emphasis on pro forma (non-GAAP, non-IFRS) earnings Both GAAP and IFRS allow managers discretion over the financial information they are required to present and over how it is presented. Analysts must be vigilant to detect managers' manipulation of financial statements which may reduce the quality of the financial statements and/or the company's earnings, even if such manipulation is not so extreme as to be criminal conduct. Analysts should pay close attention to the ratio of cash from operations (CFO) to net income. Sales on credit (ie, new accounts receivable) are included in a company's net income. Receivables must be converted to cash to pay expenses. Not converting receivables to cash may indicate that the company is recognizing "sales" that are illusory (and thus cannot be converted to cash), which is an accounting impropriety. A ratio of at least 1.0 indicates that CFO is keeping pace with net income; a ratio of consistently less than 1.0 likely constitutes a warning sign. (Choice A) Inventory turnover (ie, the ratio of COGS to average inventory) measures how quickly a company sells its inventory. If this ratio is decreasing, it may signal that the company has poor inventory management or that its inventory is becoming obsolete. Declining inventory turnover is a warning sign. (Choice B) A bill-and-hold arrangement is an agreement for a sale today with delivery deferred to a subsequent period. The seller improperly recognizes the revenue today despite not delivering the goods. Consistently using bill-and-hold transactions to recognize revenue is a warning sign.

explanation_en: Ratio analysis limitations Heterogeneous operations Inconsistent results Ratios alone are incomplete Accounting differences Analysts often using ratio analysis to assess a company's financial performance or position. Although ratio analysis may provide useful insight, it also comes with limitations: Heterogeneity in operation: If the company's divisions individually operate in distinct industries, then combining performance may oversimplify data at an aggregate level and not provide insight into divisional performance. Inconsistent interpretation of results: Different ratios may provide conflicting interpretations of performance for the same company. For example, one ratio can suggest improving liquidity whereas another ratio can suggest worsening liquidity. The need for judgment: Analysts must determine whether ratios are reliable in the context of industry and company history. Ratios are statistical measures with no inherent value and alone are incomplete; it is the analyst's interpretation that creates insight. Different accounting standards: Differences in accounting methods limit the comparability of ratios across companies. For example, one company may use FIFO inventory reporting whereas another company uses LIFO inventory reporting. Analysts must adjust company information to ensure a meaningful comparison. (Choice A) Interpretations that vary among analysts are a benefit, not a limitation, of ratio analysis. Multiple forecasts and scenarios capture a broader range of expectations. (Choice C) Adjusting results to reconcile differences in accounting standards allows for a more valid comparisons.

question_en:
A company reports the following information:

| Item | 20X5 | 20X6 |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 3.4 | 3.7 |
| Current assets | 5.0 | 5.2 |
| Current liabilities | 4.0 | 4.4 |

Based on this data, working capital turnover for 20X6 is closest to:
explanation_en: Activity ratios measure how efficiently a company utilizes its assets. The numerator is commonly an income statement item (eg revenue, COGS); the denominator is commonly a balance sheet item (eg, inventory, accounts payable). Working capital (WC) turnover measures how efficiently a company generates sales (revenue) from its current working capital. Working capital is defined as current assets (eg, accounts receivable, inventory) less current liabilities (eg, accounts payable). A high WC turnover suggests that the company is more efficient at using its short-term assets and liabilities to support sales. In this question, divide 20X6 revenue by the average working capital values to calculate working capital turnover: WC turnover(20X6) = Revenue(20X6) / [(WC(20X5) + WC(20X6)) divided by 2] = 3.7 / [(1.0 + 0.8) divided by 2] = 4.11. It is important to note that income statement items (ie, revenue) reflect what happens throughout a period, whereas balance sheet items (inventory) reflect the balance at the end of the period. Therefore, in most ratios that mix income statement with balance sheet items, the balance sheet item is averaged to better capture asset levels throughout the period. (Choice A) 3.94 results from incorrectly averaging both years' revenue in the numerator. (Choice C) 4.63 results from including only 20X6's working capital in the denominator.

question_en: A firm reports the following information (in RUB millions): Based on this data, the current year's return on common equity is closest to:
explanation_en:
Return on common equity (ROCE) gauges the amount of residual net income (after accounting for preferred dividends) generated relative to
common equity. Preferred dividends are subtracted from net income since common shareholders receive distributions only after preferred
shareholders receive their dividends. Greater ROCE ratios suggest that a company is more effective in using common equity to generate a return
for common shareholders.
ROCE should not be confused with ROE (return on equity). ROE measures the return for all equity investors (preferred and common) and is
calculated as net income / average total equity.
(Choice B) 5.18% results from failing to subtract preferred dividends from net income. ROCE measures return for common shareholders only, so
distributions to preferred shareholders (ie, preferred dividends) should be taken out.
(Choice C) 6.18% results from incorrectly using EBIT, instead of net income, in the calculation. EBIT measures profits before interest and taxes,
which reduce income available to common shareholders.

question_en: Which of the following is the best use of ratio analysis for a company?
option_a: Analyzing historical profitability ratios to make credit decisions
option_b: Analyzing current-year liquidity ratios to confirm the company's stock performance
option_c: Analyzing historical cross-sectional ratio trends to gain insights on the company's relative
explanation_en:
Insights gained from financial ratio analysis
Comprehension of: Helps in assessing:
Internal economic relationships Projected free cash flow
Current financial status Ability to expand and pay debts
Management's strategy execution Reliance on management's claims
Peer and time-series analysis Absolute and relative performance
Ratio analysis entails reviewing a company's activity, leverage, profitability, and valuation ratios. Detecting important economic connections
between different ratios is crucial in making economic decisions; the ratios alone are just statistics regarding a company's performance.
Analysts seek connections between ratios from time-series or cross-sectional analyses. A company's efficiency may impact its profitability, which
in turn affects its valuation. Analysts must use inferences from ratio analyses to form independent judgments. They then use these judgments to
arrive at economic conclusions (eg, creditworthiness, stock price).
(Choice A) Historical profitability ratios show the company's ability to generate profit, but since profit is different from cash flow, these ratios are
not useful in determining the company's creditworthiness.
(Choice B) The current year's liquidity ratios are data that may indicate the company's ability to pay short-term debts. Only a comprehensive
evaluation of all ratios over time can provide an understanding of the company's overall performance, not just its liquidity.

Liquidity ratios measure how well a company can cover its short-term obligations with cash or assets that are easily converted to cash.
Solvency ratios measure a company's ability to satisfy its long-term obligations.
Profitability ratios measure a company's return on sales and return on investments.
Valuation ratios measures a company's stock price relative to its fundamentals.

question_en:
A consultant gathers the following profitability ratios for a company:

| Profitability Ratio (%) | 20X1 | 20X2 | 20X3 |

| Operating profit margin | 10.10 | 10.00 | 8.90 |
| Pretax margin | 9.90 | 9.90 | 6.90 |

Based on this information, over this period the company most likely improved its ability to cover:
explanation_en:
Profit margins (profit / revenue) indicate a company's ability to generate adequate sales to cover various costs:
Gross margin measures ability to cover COGS, which are costs directly attributable to producing the goods and services sold (eg, raw
material costs, production wages, distribution costs).
Operating margin measures ability to further cover operating expenses such as marketing or research and development.
Pretax margin measures ability to further cover certain nonoperating expenses such as financing costs (eg, interest).
Net margin measures ability to further cover taxes.
In this scenario, gross margin increased over time, which means the company improved its ability to cover COGS, including raw material costs.
(Choice B) Operating margin decreased over time, which suggests a worsened ability to cover operating expenses.
(Choice C) Pretax margin remained unchanged, which suggests deterioration or no improvement in the company's ability to cover nonoperating
expenses (before taxes).

question_en:
An analyst collects the following annual data for a company:

| | Company | Industry Average |
|---|---|---|
| Days of sales outstanding | 45.10 | 30.09 |
| Total asset turnover | 1.20 | 1.15 |
| Days of inventory on hand | 25.42 | 29.77 |

Which of the following best describes how the company's efficiency compares with the industry?
option_a: The company has a receivable turnover that is better.
option_b: The company has more effective inventory management.
option_c: The company produces less revenue for a given asset level.
explanation_en:
Activity ratios measure how efficient a company is and indicate its operational performance. Days of inventory on hand (DOH), an activity ratio,
indicates management's effectiveness in overseeing its inventory. DOH is the average number of days it takes a company to convert inventory
(eg, current assets) into revenue.
The ratio is calculated as the number of days in the period divided by the company's inventory turnover (COGS/average inventory). Lower DOH
suggests that management has a lower drain on company assets and generates revenue more quickly. Here, it has more effective inventory
management than its peers since its DOH is less than the industry average (25.42 < 29.77).
(Choice A) Using the days of sales outstanding formula, the company's receivable turnover of 8.09 (45.10 = 365 / receivable turnover) is lower
than the industry's of 12.13 (30.09 = 365/receivable turnover). Its receivable turnover is worse, not better than the industry average. If the days of
sales outstanding (DSO) is lower than the industry average, so is the receivable turnover since they are effectively the same; DSO converts
turnover into a time measurement.
(Choice C) Total asset turnover is a ratio that measures a company's overall efficiency; a higher ratio means the company is more efficient at
generating revenue for a given level of assets. The company produces more revenue for a given asset level than its peers since its total asset
turnover is greater (1.20 > 1.15) than the industry average.

question_en:
An analyst completes the following DuPont analysis on two companies:

|  | Company X | Company Y |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tax burden | 0.75 | 0.75 |
| Interest burden | 0.80 | 0.80 |
| EBIT margin | 0.10 | 0.18 |
| Asset turnover | 0.90 | 1.20 |
| Leverage | 3.00 | 1.20 |

Compared with Company Y, Company X mostly likely has a:
option_a: lower ROE and is more efficient.
option_b: higher ROE and has a higher profit margin.
option_c: higher ROE and a higher proportion of debt.
explanation_en:
DuPont analysis entails decomposing ROE into five components. In this case, multiply the five components together to find the ROE of
Companies X and Y, which are 16.20% and 15.55%, respectively. Company X has a higher ROE despite its lower profitability (0.10 vs. 0.18) and
efficiency (0.90 vs. 1.20) compared with Company Y's. Company X has greater leverage (ie, proportion of debt) than Company Y (3.00 vs 1.20),
which is why Company X's ROE is greater than Company Y's (Choices A and B).
Leverage is a gauge of solvency as measured by the company's assets relative to its average total equity. The higher the ratio, the more the
company finances its assets with debt.

question_en:
A company uses LIFO to determine the valuation for inventory and reports the following under US GAAP:

| Selected Items from Financial Statements | 20X7 | 20X6 |
|---|---|---|
| Current assets (USD millions) | 1,400 | 1,660 |
| Current liabilities (USD millions) | 333 | 400 |

The company discloses that its LIFO reserve in 20X7 was $277 and in 20X6 was $450. If the company used FIFO instead of LIFO for its inventory valuation, then over the last year, the company's current ratio most likely:
explanation_en: FIFO inventory = Inventory valued under LIFO + LIFO reserve. Companies that use LIFO (last-in, first-out) to value inventory often report lower inventory and higher expense than companies that use FIFO (first-in, first-out). Under US GAAP, companies that use LIFO must report the difference between inventory under LIFO and FIFO as the LIFO reserve. When preparing comparisons between companies that differ in their use of LIFO and FIFO inventory valuation, add back the LIFO reserve to convert LIFO inventory to FIFO. In this case, to find the company's current ratio as it would be under the FIFO method, add the LIFO reserve to current assets (inventory is a part of current assets). Adjusted current assets: 20X7: 1,400 + 277 = 1,677; 20X6: 1,680 + 450 = 2,130. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Using current assets adjusted for FIFO, the current ratio decreases year over year from 5.33 to 5.04: 20X7: 1,677 / 333 = 5.04; 20X6: 2,130 / 400 = 5.33. (Choice B) The current ratio would have remained the same with no adjustment for differences in the accounting method. (Choice C) The current ratio would have increased by subtracting the LIFO reserve from current assets. To adjust for differences between LIFO and FIFO, add the LIFO reserves to inventory. This increases current assets. Things to remember: When comparing companies, some of which use LIFO and some of which use FIFO for inventory reporting, make their inventory values comparable by adding the LIFO reserve to the LIFO inventory valuation.
